title: The Exxon Valdez Was Operated With a Reduced Crew Complement. Its Lookout Routinely Went Unattended.
title_candidates: Exxon Operated the Exxon Valdez With a Reduced Crew. The Lookout Routinely Went Unattended.
The Exxon Valdez Was Operated With a Reduced Crew Complement. Its Lookout Routinely Went Unattended.
The Safety Board Said the Exxon Valdez Lookout Routinely Went Unattended. The Manning Was Reduced.
description:
There is a number written on a piece of paper for every ship at sea. It is the smallest number of people the ship is allowed to sail with.

For one tanker in Alaska, that number was worked out for a voyage to Panama. By the winter of 1989 she was not going to Panama any more. The number had not moved.

On the night of the twenty-fourth of March, 1989, at nine minutes past midnight, the third mate is the officer with navigational control of a loaded crude oil tanker in Prince William Sound, Alaska. The National Transportation Safety Board's summary of his previous twenty-four hours is one sentence long. He "had probably had very little sleep the night before the grounding and had worked a stressful, physically demanding day."

He went to bed some time after one in the morning on the twenty-third. His bed was fifty feet from a cargo operation. He could have had as little as four hours of sleep before starting the workday on the twenty-third, and a one- to two-hour nap. As little as five or six hours in the previous twenty-four. And at the moment we are talking about, he was working beyond his normal watch period.

The document that states a cause for this grounding is a two-hundred-and-fifty-seven-page report that could not be read for this film. So this film does not tell you why the ship grounded. It tells you why she went to sea with a tired crew, which the record does say, at length, in the Board's own words.

A tanker of this kind carries three deck officers below the master. A ship at sea never stops, so somebody has to be on the bridge for every one of the twenty-four hours. Four on, eight off. Now take one of the three away. Divide twenty-four hours between two people and each stands twelve. Six on, six off, twice a day. It "seldom enables any officer to acquire adequate rest until the vessel returns to sea."

When the ship is in port loading or discharging, the chief mate runs the cargo. The Board says plainly that this is widely practised.

The EXXON VALDEZ was operated with a reduced crew complement, and the Board states that evidence indicated watchkeeping safeguards had been compromised because of the manning level. "As a result, on the EXXON VALDEZ, the lookout position routinely went unattended when the AB was called for other tasks or took a break." Routinely. Not once.

When the minimum crew requirements were established for the EXXON VALDEZ, the vessel had been scheduled for the Valdez-to-Panama trade. That trade was discontinued after December 1988. And the ship began operating regularly between Valdez and ports in California. A much shorter passage. The same number of people. "The mates on the EXXON VALDEZ were usually fatigued after cargo handling operations in Valdez, and the vessel usually put to sea with a fatigued crew."

The Board's verdict on the reduced manning practices of the company: they are "generally incautious and without apparent justification from the standpoint of safety."

Then six recommendations. Four of six are about hours, manning and watch-keeping. Two are about the alcohol programme, and both of those are about supervision, not about the drink. And they were not sent to Exxon. They were addressed to all shipping companies operating in Prince William Sound.

Exxon spent some two point one billion dollars on cleanup. It settled a civil action by the United States and Alaska for at least nine hundred million. The case became a class of thirty-two thousand people. In one phase, the jury awarded two hundred and eighty-seven million dollars in compensatory damages to some of them. Then the jury turned to punishment. It awarded five thousand dollars against the master. And five billion dollars against the company.

The Ninth Circuit ultimately remitted the award to two and a half billion. The Court named the real problem instead: "the stark unpredictability of punitive awards." So it held that in maritime cases like this one, a ratio of one to one between punitive and compensatory damages is a fair upper limit. One dollar of punishment for one dollar of harm. It then took for granted the District Court's calculation of the total relevant compensatory damages: five hundred and seven and a half million dollars.

The judgment was vacated and remanded on the twenty-fifth of June, 2008. Nineteen years after the grounding.

—

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from a National Transportation Safety Board safety recommendation letter and from the Supreme Court's opinion in this case, read in full. The Board's main accident report is a photographic scan with no machine-readable text in it and was not read for this film, so this film states no probable cause for the grounding.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
_built: 2026-08-27 by the design thread. DESCRIPTION LENGTH: 4,928 characters, against YouTube's 5,000 ceiling, which check_packaging_qc now enforces as a hard problem. The first draft was 5,591 and would have been rejected by the upload call after the render. Seven whole sentences were cut, never clauses, so that every surviving claim is still a sentence the script speaks: the framing line 'This is a film about what a crew number actually promises' (restates the opening), 'He may have been called as early as twenty past five that morning' (one of three consecutive sleep-arithmetic sentences), 'It is a photographic scan with no machine-readable text in it...' (the closing source note says the same thing), 'Divide that among three officers and each stands eight hours...' and 'The Board's sentence about that arrangement contains no adjectives at all' (derivation and lead-in that the following lines carry anyway), 'If the chief mate is doing cargo, he is not standing his in-port watch. And on a three-mate ship there are only two other people.' (restates 'Now take one of the three away' from the paragraph above), and 'And it paid another three hundred and three million in voluntary payments to private parties' (third of three money-already-paid sentences). Kept deliberately: the searchable case name, the manning finding, the lookout sentence, the one-to-one ratio, and the AI-disclosure line. Title and description are written out of 03_script/script.en.v001.md's own sentences rather than paraphrased, because paraphrase is what check_packaging_claims flags as unverified; every claim in both comes back SUPPORTED with a file:line citation. The thumbnail wording is declared under `thumbnail_text` (not `thumbnail_headline`, as EP80 used) so that check_packaging_claims._thumb_text actually reads it -- it only picks up keys containing both 'thumb' and 'text', and 'ONE TO ONE.' is the wording burned into all three thumbnail candidates on disk. Nothing here states a probable cause for the grounding: MAR-90/04 is a 257-page scan with no text layer and has not been read (episode_spec forbidden_claims, first entry). Nothing says the master was drunk at the wheel, that fatigue caused the grounding, that Exxon was uniquely bad among tanker operators, that any recommendation was ever adopted, or that the Supreme Court let the company off -- the money it had already spent is stated alongside the ratio rule for exactly that reason.
